Each panel has its own color scale (nats).

figures.caption: Experimental priorities depend on the causal question. In this six-node example, the target is the effect of setting X3 to 10 on X5 and X6. Learning all model parameters ranks an intervention on X1 highest; targeting the causal query instead ranks X3 highest. The panels retain the paper’s original information-gain values and rankings.

figures.caption: Which measurements would best inform a turbulence model? These maps show mean information-gain estimates from 22 repeated multifidelity estimation trials near a flat plate. The right panel uses a logarithmic vertical coordinate to reveal the near-wall structure. Color represents the estimated information gain, rather than velocity or prediction error.

files.alt: Estimator variance falls initially and then rises as more of a fixed computational budget is spent on pilot sampling.
Predicted and actual estimator variance differ sharply with very few pilot samples and become closer as pilot sampling increases.

figures.caption: Pilot sampling has both a benefit and a cost. In this benchmark, too little pilot data leads to poor allocation, while too much leaves insufficient budget for the final estimate (left). A small pilot sample can also yield overconfident variance predictions (right). Dashed lines mark single-fidelity Monte Carlo and exact-covariance reference cases.
figures.alt: Estimator variance falls initially and then rises as more of a fixed computational budget is spent on pilot sampling. Predicted and actual estimator variance differ sharply with very few pilot samples and become closer as pilot sampling increases.
